To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the mere presence of a person in a position that allows action on objects on a table induces a good proportion of people to take the person's perspective on the location of the objects and (2) when a query is posed in terms of action rather than location, more people spontaneously take the other's perspective on the objects.

(a) the mere presence of another in a position to take action induced a good proportion (50-60%) of respondents to describe spatial relations from that other's perspective; (b) this effect was not due to a tendency to describe spatial relations in the same way as they would be described from the other's perspective, but was due to a shift in the perspective from which the description was made; and (c) when the query about the scene's spatial relations was ph rased in terms
(a) people can take spatial perspective of another person in the absence of a specific instruction to do so, and that (b) this is more likely to happen when the query is about action.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people take the perspectives of others in order to understand their actions.
how people understand others and how others understand people.
the embodied nature of cognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of another person, especially when the query is phrased in a way that implies action, induces spatial perspective-taking.
spatial perspective-taking is not a matter of egocentricity, as is commonly thought, but a matter of action and intentionality.
the mere presence of another human being induces spontaneous spatial perspective-taking in the service of action understanding.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mere presence of a person in a position of action elicits a spontaneous shift in spatial perspectives, which can be understood in terms of the theory of embodied cognition.
we are able to take the perspective of others, even when they are not present, and that this is not a conscious effort but a spontaneous response to an implication of action.
the human mind is embodied and disembodied, and that it is both egocentric and allocentric.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mere presence of an actor in an action scene can elicit spontaneous perspective-taking, even when that person is not the intended agent of the described action.
the mere implication of action can induce spontaneous perspective-taking, seemingly to understand the other's action, even when there is no explicit request to do so.

the mere presence of a person who is in a position to interact with objects induces a good proportion of people to describe the spatial relation between those objects from the person's point of vantage, as if the person is acting on those objects.
